### layers of forwarding (incoming MTA) 

![](/smtp/texfig/smtp-relay-mtainput.figure.svg){fig-alt="diagram of mail going from user@sender.com to user@receiver.com seen earlier, with incoming MTA for sender.com highlighted. The mail submission agent that user@receiver.com used sends the message via SMTP to the incoming MTA. The incoming MTA forwards the message to one of several backend servers (a ticketing system, mailing list system, user mail system) based on its address. It also checks SPF and DKIM info and antispam databases."}

# anti-spam

### layers of forwarding

![](/smtp/texfig/smtp-relay.figure.svg){fig-alt="mail from mail user agent for user@sender.com goes to mail submission agent via SMTP. The mail submission agent uses SMTP to send to an incoming MTA at receiver.com, looking up that incoming MTA via an MX record. That MTA looks SPF and DKIM information via DNS and consults antispam databases. It forwards using SMTP based on the RCPT address to either a ticketing system, mailing list system, and/or user mail system. The user mail system communicates messages to a mail user agent for user@receiver.com via POP3 or IMAP or similar."}

### SMTP and TLS

*  SMTP historically not encrypted
   *  typical idea: mail messages should be encrypted if needed
   *  (but hard to encrypt header information usefully....)
*  "opportunistic"
   *  look for "STARTTLS" command being supported
      *  EHLO response will indicate if supported
   *  hope not interfered with by attacker
*  MTA-STS: mechanism to indicate (via DNS + HTTPS) to use TLS with SMTP
